title: 13 — Gravity without Absolutes
paragraphs: Julian Barbour

Newton formulated his laws of universal gravitation in the reductionist framework of absolute space and time. As a result his equations, when used to model a universe as opposed to subsystems within it, allow vastly more solutions, with a matching loss of predictability, than in a purely relational holistic setting. A similar loss of predictability may also be present in general relativity since in infinitesimal regions spacetime is Minkowskian with an absolute structure. In fact, the reductionism physics inherited from Newton may give a seriously wrong picture of reality and the universe.

Expanded text of online talk for the Time in Physics International Workshop, São Paulo, Brazil, 13/05/2025. This essay will appear, in a possibly extended form, in a book currently being written by Julian Barbour and Maria Lourenço.
Introduction

In 1999, aiming to liberate dynamics from Newton’s absolutes, I defined [1], for finitely many point particles with given mass ratios, shape space S as the analogue of the Newtonian configuration space N but for the shapes that points can define. The simplest examples are triangles or tetrahedra; two points do not define a shape. Shape space S is the quotient of N with respect to (wrt) the similarity group Sim. Newtonian solutions can be ‘projected’ to S as undirected unparametrised curves without loss of any intrinsic information. The ‘shape dynamics’ that results is timeless: history is a curve in S, not a point moving along it at some speed as measured by an invisible absolute time. Such a ‘speed’ is obtained using the ephemeris time that in the 1890s astronomers, doubting the reliability of the sidereal time that the Earth’s rotation defines, introduced as a parameter with respect to which evolution unfolds in accordance with Newton’s 2nd law (see [2]).

The distinguishing aspect of the quotienting wrt Sim is the inclusion of dilatations, which do not belong to the Euclidean group. The Newtonian gravitational potential V_(New) is not scale invariant; in fact, nothing in modern physics and cosmology is except for a little known part of Newtonian gravity to which I will come. It is not difficult to see that the neglect is suspect. Consider any triangle. It will have a shape that its internal angles define and a size that can be increased or decreased without changing the angles. They are scale invariant. The same distinction exists for any number of points distributed in Euclidean space. From any point, the lines to any other two make an angle. Overall expansion will not change any of those angles. It is often forgotten, or not even realised, that within any system only angles are observable. Size presupposes an external ruler and has no objective meaning for a totality such as we take the universe to be. Ratios determine reality. That fact is especially clear on a moonless night. All we see are ratios of angles between the stars, all of which are fractions of 2π, the measure of great circles on the sky. Reality is relational; the laws we use to describe it should be scale invariant. It is remarkable that they are not. I will return to this fact.
Newton’s ‘Corruption’ of His Theory

It is arguable that Newton’s greatest achievement was the formulation of his second law of motion. It determines how forces change motion. However, to be applied initial positions and velocities, or an equivalent amount of information, must be supplied. Suppose we want to determine possible histories of the simplest non-trivial example of a Newtonian universe, which corresponds to the three-body problem: three particles that in relational terms are expressed at any instant by two independently specifiable mass ratios and two internal angles of the triangle they form. At any instant the relational information about the particles, besides the mass ratios (assumed given), will take the form of the shape of the triangle that they form. That is enough to specify purely nominal Cartesian coordinates for the particles; the only restriction on them is that they must correspond to the given shape. Now suppose also given a slightly different shape of the triangle. There will be an _irreducible difference_ between the shapes, which I will call Apple and Pear to avoid implying one comes before the other. The problem with the notions of absolute time and space, which latter includes an implicit absolute scale, is that they permit specification, from the same irreducible difference, a huge range of different initial data with which the second law can generate evolution. Arbitrariness enters as follows:
Does Apple or Pear come first in time and how much time dt is between them.
What is the angle dω between them (three degrees of freedom: one for the magnitude of the angle and two for its direction).
What is the ratio of the centre-of-mass moments of inertia.

I have not included the distance dx between their centres of mass since, provided the potential does not depend on the position of the system in absolute space, Galilean relativity will ensure the evolution does not depend on it. However, items 1–3 all bring in arbitrariness.

As regards the precedence in time in 1, it will be established when the other arbitrary elements have been eliminated, so we turn to them. Whether Apple or Pear is assumed to come first in time, the nominal coordinates chosen for it fix the potential energy V. But since dt is unknown, so too is the initial kinetic energy T and with it the total energy E. That brings in a one-parameter arbitrariness in the resulting evolution. How can we eliminate it?

For this, we turn to Newton’s contemporary Wilhelm Gottfried Leibniz, who not only advocated relational concepts of space and time but also, for related reasons, differed from Newton in being committed to the idea that we live in a rational universe. This led the two men to disagree about what might be called the ultimate reasons for things, for which both regarded God to be the arbiter. Newton believed God had complete freedom to do whatever he liked, but for Leibniz God would always have a reason for any choice he made and would choose the best option available. This led him to formulate what he regarded as his most important principle concerning contingent facts and called the principle of sufficient reason (PSR). According to it, no fact can hold, or a proposition be true, unless there is a reason for it.[1] Leibniz recognised that in general it would be difficult to find the reason for a particular contingent fact. I do not know if he mentioned it, but the difficulty is much reduced if numbers are associated with a range of possibilities. This is for the simple reason that some numbers are distinguished; π is one and so is e. However, the three that help in the problem with _N_-body initial data are the most special of all: 0,1 , and ∞.

Let us see how they solve the problem with the energy E. If initially we choose E = ∞, the system will be blown apart instantly; 1 cannot be invoked in this case because it is not a scale-invariant value of the energy, which has dimensions; in contrast, E = 0 is a scale-invariant fact and gives a perfectly sensible solution: only solutions with vanishing energy are allowed.[2] Exactly the same is true for problem 2, which means that the magnitude and direction (relative to the initial shape) are undetermined and we have three further arbitrary elements; they too can be eliminated simply by requiring the angular momentum to be zero: L = 0.

It is when we come to the third problem that the application of the PSR has its greatest effect. Although we can say that the centre-of-mass moment of inertia I_(cm) is zero at both instants, that will not yield a sensible solution. However, the ratio of the values of I_(cm) at the two instants can be 1, which is both scale-invariant and satisfies the PSR. This possibility, realised by geodesic motion on shape space S, is explored in my [3] but, as noted there, found wanting since it cannot satisfactorily reproduce expansion of the universe. It was recently pointed out to me by Pooya Farokhi that there is a shape-related reason for that. Whereas the Newtonian configuration space N is non-compact, which means that I_(cm) can become infinite (thereby allowing the universe to expand without limit in absolute space), shape space S is compact because the quotienting of N by Sim includes dilatationsa and that makes S compact. This, in turn, means that geodesics on S are Poincaré recurrent and cannot be associated with an arrow of time, in contrast to, as I will shortly explain, the solutions we obtain after we have eliminated all Newtonian solutions that fail the ‘no-absolutes’ test.

Addressing that problem, I note that we have already reduced the _N_-body solutions otherwise regarded as allowed to the zero-measure set with both energy E and angular momentum L zero. Can we reduce them even further? We can. Here again Leibniz helps because it was his idea—that God would achieve his aims with the least effort—which led to the development of the principle of least action, long regarded as the foundational principle of dynamics. Among other conditions, it requires that at the limits of integration there must be a finite ratio, neither 0 nor ∞, of the quantity that measures the scale of the system, which is the square root of the centre-of-mass moment of inertia I_(cm). This poses the following question: do _N_-body solutions exist that do not satisfy this condition? The answer is yes.

Karl Sundman [4] found the first in the three-body problem in 1907 and Block extended them to arbitrary _N_ a year later [5]. They are called total-collision solutions because in them √(I_(cm)), the extrinsic Newtonian scale implicit in the notion of absolute space,[3] vanishes at a certain stage in the evolution, beyond which no unique way to continue the solutions has been found and it is assumed Newton’s equations breakdown. For a total collision to happen, two conditions must be satisfied. First, the total angular momentum must be zero (there is no restriction on the energy) and, second, the system must reach the shape of what is called a central configuration or relative equilibrium. Such shapes have great interest, so, in a somewhat extended digression, I will say something about them that reading Leibniz’s _Monadology_ in 1977 led me many years later, in 2011, to an interesting way to find them.

In his slim booklet, which takes the form of 90 aphoristic paragraphs, Leibniz proposes a form of idealism based on the notion of monads, the name taken from the Greek _monas_ already used by the Pythagoreans for “the One”, the divine principle of reality, representing unity, the origin of all numbers, and the source of all things. According to Leibniz, a monad is a simple substance, that is, something without parts. However, the monads have structure through which they all ‘mirror’ each other and thereby constitute the universe. The mirroring holds them together by what Leibniz called the pre-established harmony with which God brought them into existence at the creation and maintained ever after like two clocks that, once started, keep perfect time together through eternity. As an illustration of his universe of monads, Leibniz points out that the same town seen from different sides appears quite different and is, as it were, multiplied in perspective which, however, merely gives different views of the same town. He says that, in the case of monads, “this is the means of obtaining as much variety as possible, but with the greatest order possible; that is to say it is the means of obtaining as much perfection as possible.” In Leibniz’s holistic and entirely idealistic scheme, the views of the town introduce geometry, but only by analogy. The geometry suggested to me a few years ago the following way to define variety, which Leibniz rated so highly.

Consider three or more points in (Euclidean) space; what scaleinvariant number characterises the extent to which they are uniformly distributed or clustered? To be scale-invariant, it must have length dimension zero. That is readily achieved by making it the ratio of two numbers that the complete set of points define and each have length dimension one. Mathematically two such numbers are distinguished: the root-mean-square length ℓ_(rms), which is proportional to √(I_(cm)), and the mean-harmonic length ℓ_(mhl). Then the scale-invariant number I call the _variety_ V, since Leibniz was the inspiration for finding it,[4] is

The variety V is manifestly a scale-invariant ratio. As such, it has an important property: for any nominal scale used to define distances and with them an _extrinsic_ scale of the system, the large separations dominate the first factor and the short ones the second. Thus, except for a fractional residue, the variety is the number of times a shorter length fits into a longer one. This is exactly what happens in measurement. Thus, the variety measures the _intrinsic_ size of the universe that the points define. Moreover, the expanded form, with each term ℓ_(rms) divided by just one two-particle separation, is very interesting. It makes V exceptionally sensitive to a reduction in any one of the two-point separations because then the corresponding term, and with it V, can become arbitrarily large, even infinite.

In this connection, consider the following problem: find distributions of _N_ points with, say, N ≥ 50 (the value at which interesting effects become manifest), for which V has a value that lies within a narrow preassigned range above the absolute minimum which, as a positive-definite function, it has. It is clear that it will be very easy to ‘overshoot’ the value—too close proximity of any two points will do that. Moreover, the expanded form of (13.3) shows that ‘hitting’ the target value involves the achievement of a delicate holistic balance that is established mainly between the shortest separations especially if many particles are involved. This is because ℓ_(rms), the numerator of each of the terms in (13.3), is only weakly sensitive to a pair of particles getting closer to each other, but exactly the opposite is true for any of the denominators.

I now come to the connection with Newtonian gravity. Since 1999, I have been lucky to interact with specialists in the _N_-body problem of Newton’s theory and, thanks to them, I learned in 2011 that, with sign reversed, the variety (13.3) plays an important role in it and is called the shape potential or normalised Newton potential. To explain why, let me say that the points are particles and, as in the following expression for the factors in the variety, replace the letters a,b,c,…,… by Euclidean separations r_(ij) and add masses m_i that are a fraction of a nominal unit total mass, ∑_(i)m_i = 1. Then
ℓ_(rms) = √(∑_(i < j)m_im_jr_(ij)²),
where r_(ij) is the distance between the points i and j,
ℓ_(mhl)⁻¹ = ∑_(i < j)m_im_j/(r_(ij)),

The numerator in the variety (13.4) then becomes the mass-weighted measure of the size of any Newtonian _N_-body system; the denominator is minus the inverse of the Newton potential V_(New). The minus sign is purely nominal; without it, V_(New) is often called the force function.

Several comments are here in order. First, everything of interest already holds for equal-mass particles. They, like particles with different masses, can be treated, as in my heuristic derivation of the variety, as points with zero size. Second, as just shown, the zero size of points, with or without mass, makes satisfaction of scale invariance trivial along with the formation of structures in the form of clusters of points. I find it hard to imagine a simpler ontology that is capable of modelling in scale-invariant terms our experience of structures around us and in the universe at large. A third and final comment is this. The simplest way to define the variety of points in space, which Leibniz himself could have proposed, leads directly to the two functions that define the oldest non-trivial dynamical theory: the _N_-body problem of Newton’s theory of universal gravitation. Simply defining how particle separations change in a scale-invariant manner by means of two functions, nothing more, nothing less, unifies the aspirations of those two bitter enemies. That ends my digression, the reason for which is that the special shape, a configuration, that must be the terminus of a total-collision solution corresponds to a critical value of the variety (13.3)—the absolute minimum (the most interesting case as we will see), a local minimum, or a saddle.

The condition that the terminal shape must be critical shows that the moniker total collision is unfortunate since it suggests all the points really do collide at a single point, moreover with infinite speed. But if we insist only the possible shapes of Newtonian universes are real, total collision gives a misleading impression for which Newton’s absolute space and the intuition that goes with it is responsible. It is true that ℓ_(rms) vanishes, but this is not something which observers within the universe could register. What they could is that their universe is in a special shape, equilateral or collinear in the three-body problem, or one of the great number, possibly infinite, critical shapes known as central configurations (and also relative equilibria).[5] Their number is an issue that I will address shortly, but first I must mention counterparts of total-collision solutions that are called parabolic-escape solutions. Jean Chazy discovered them in the three-body in the 1920s. In them, the energy must be zero but the angular momentum can have any value. They too terminate in a shape for which the variety has a critical value. However, in the Newtonian representation instead of all the particles colliding with infinite speed on top of each with zero distance between any two of them, in the parabolic-escape solutions all the particles come to rest infinitely far apart.

These two kinds of solution are obviously already very special, but what about the solutions that, in the Newtonian representation, are total-collision solutions with zero energy or parabolic-escape solutions with vanishing angular momentum? How will they appear when represented, without, as I said earlier, any loss of essential information, as unparametrised and undirected curves in shape space S? Will it be possible to tell the two apart? No. In both cases, there will just be a curve in S that terminates at one end as a central configuration and extends forever away from it through shapes whose variety increases progressively if not strictly monotonically.

These solutions are particularly interesting in two respects. The first is that by the time-reversal symmetry of Newton’s laws, both can be interpreted as Newtonian big bangs. Their mathematical structure, if not their interpretation, was established before Hubble’s observations showed that the universe is expanding (by two decades in the case of total-collision solutions). It is also worth noting that the actual state of the universe at the first instant of time is not well defined in general relativity but it and the nature of the subsequent evolution is in the Newtonian big-bang solutions.[6] I will return to this when considering the implications of the ‘no-absolutes’ approach in the context of Einstein’s theory. The second respect in which the considered solutions have great interest is that they solve the longstanding problem of how there can be an arrow of time despite the time-reversal symmetry of Newton’s equations; their arrow is defined by the direction of increasing variety from the central configuration, which can be taken as their first instant.[7] At the same time they match well in qualitative terms the known history of the universe from its conjectured big-bang origin to the present day.

The presence of an emergent arrow of time resolves the problem whose resolution I postponed at the start of this discussion—given the irreducible difference of two shapes from which possible Newtonian initial data are to be constructed, which comes first in time? Within the now greatly reduced set of such initial data, the answer follows with necessity. A direction of time that corresponds to growth of structure and complexity exists in _all_ the solutions that our principles allow. On that basis we can say which of the two shapes comes first in time as revealed by actual structure as opposed to Newton’s absolute time, which takes reductionism to its _ne plus ultra_: an undirected line of indistinguishable points. In the scale-invariant shape-based approach, that is replaced by shapes of ever changing structures. Shapes are the true instants of time. As explained in [2], duration—Newton’s time—is an emergent magnitude whose introduction as independent variable make the evolution through the pre-existing successive shapes match the form of Newton’s second law.

It is not only the problem of the time-reversal symmetry that is resolved in the approach based on shapes. At the level of objective reality, with all absolutes removed, a problem related to scale appears and is resolved. When shorn of the artificial and reductionist scaffolding of absolutes, Newton’s second law of motion (the expression of how forces change motion) is, as explained above, seen to define a direction—the one in which variety increases. Will it also define a direction of increasing size as well as variety? I do not see how it can. If the critical shape at one end is taken to be the first shape of a Newtonian big bang (the time-reverse of a total collision), then its size, measured by √(I_(cm)), will be zero. But if it is taken to be at the end of parabolic escape, then √(I_(cm)) will be infinite. As Newton formulated his equations, this shows that the only solutions which should be retained are not only time-reversal invariant but also scale-inversion invariant. In fact, the true core of Newton’s theory, seen without all the dubious elements he added to it, is very simple. It suggests a universe whose first instant is a shape more uniform shape than all the successive shapes that become ever more varied as defined by (13.3) in the case of equal masses and (13.4) with mass ratios.

But we have still not exhausted what the PSR can do. I mentioned in footnote 5 that it is not known whether the number of central configurations, for given _N_, is finite or infinite. At the very least there are a great many, factorial already for those that are collinear. With increase of the variety chosen to define the direction of time, all these central configurations could be first instants of the solutions that, in Newtonian terms, could be either total collision or parabolic escape. Here again the PSR can be invoked—only those candidate solutions for which the variety of their first instant has the absolute minimum value are to be considered. I think this is as far as the PSR can take us since, except in the case of relatively small _N_, it is not known if there is a unique shape that has the minimum value of the variety.

This concludes my discussion of how Newton’s absolutes allows his second law of motion to have vastly more solutions than it should. But besides the loss of predictability, it can be argued that the ‘quality’ of the solutions is reduced. Of course, I must explain what I mean by quality. I mean ‘how long’ something of interest continues to unfold in solutions. This can be illustrated nicely in the three-body problem. All solutions for which both the energy and angular momentum are zero have a very characteristic structure. In whatever direction Newtonian time is assumed to flow, in the infinitely distant past the size of the system measured by √(I_(cm)) is infinitely great and decreases monotonically to a finite value after which it increases monotonically to an infinite value again. The size of the system is not of much interest, being, as I said, unobservable within the system. What is interesting is the form of the solution. In the distant past it consists of two particles orbiting their centre of mass in Keplerian elliptical orbits while a single particle, which I will call the singleton, approaches it in the opposite direction from an infinite distance and satisfies to very good accuracy Newton’s first law of motion. As the two parts of the system approach each other, three-body interaction becomes effective and acts as a perfect scrambler. At the least, the orbital elements of the pair will be changed and the singleton will have its energy changed. However, in a more dramatic effect, there may be a swapping of partners and two new particles will form a different Kepler pair. Either side of the scrambler, we have bidirectional arrows of time defined by the formation of the pair, which becomes a rod, clock, and compass all in one. In the limit, the pair becomes an ‘instrument’ that measures with ever better accuracy the speed and direction of the singleton leaving it in the opposite direction. For the _N_-body problem with N > 3, multiple Kepler pairs can form with periods that become ever better synchronised. That is what I mean by quality of a solution. In contrast, typical 3-body solutions with energy greater than zero are likely to break up as √(I_(cm)) reaches infinity.

Extensive numerical simulations of _N_-body solutions with more than three particles would be needed to see how long they remain “interesting”. Some work along this line has been done by my collaborator Hemant Shukla, and does indeed show that only solutions with vanishing energy and angular momentum are likely to remain interesting over an extended period. These numerical solutions and the results reported in [8] even suggest how laws of Nature can, without ever holding exactly, arise from a ‘law of the universe’. This is because the ‘uncorrupted’ solutions with E = L = 0 satisfy that condition forever but both in the big-bang solutions and ‘Janus-point’ solutions with bidirectional arrows of time (discussed in more detail in [14]) break up into subsystems that can have all possible approximately conserved energies, momenta, and angular momenta proved the totals are all zero. The subsystems satisfy emergent local laws of motion in an inertial frame that the complete universe defines.
Conclusion

There is much more that could be said about Newton’s absolutes, but I will restrict myself to a few concluding comments. The first is that they hugely reduce the predictive strength of his own fundamental law of motion and may have given a completely wrong impression of what reality and the universe are like. Indeed, one sees that in the etymology of real, which derives from the Latin _res_, for thing, and a thing can only be recognised as such if it has attributes. Newton’s invisible space and time have none, or at least none that can be actually registered. Newton’s reductionism made that impossible. Now the same defect may be hidden in the foundations of general relativity. Although its fundamental concept, spacetime, undoubtedly has genuine structure expressed through curvature, it ’disappears’ in infinitesimal regions where it must become Minkowskian and, as Einstein commented, Minkowski space, which glues space and time together, is as absolute as Newton’s space and time are separately.

Conceptually, apart from the role ascribed to light, ontology had not changed where it counts. One sees this in Minkowski’s famous lecture of 1908, in which he said “The objects of our perception invariably include places and times in combination. Nobody has ever noticed a place except at a time, or a time except at a place.” Here there are already problems. How are places and times noticed, or, more fundamentally, how are they defined? Moreover, do places and times, as Minkowski clearly implies, have equal ontological status? That is questionable. Without the hand of a clock, we cannot tell the time. More fundamentally, any objective notion of place is relative. We need to be able to see things to know where we are; writing in the same period as Minkowski, Poincaré put great emphasis on that [6,7]. In the text immediately following the words I have quoted, Minkowski could avoid those problems because, when he gave his lecture, he was standing in front of a blackboard and was able to say: “A point of space at a point of time, that is, a system of values x,y, z,t, I will call a _world-point_. The multiplicity of all thinkable x,y,z,t systems of values we will christen the _world_. With this most valiant piece of chalk I might project upon the blackboard four world-axes.” All very confident. However Minkowski does exhibit some unease about his scheme because he says: “Not to leave a yawning void anywhere, we will imagine that everywhere and everywhen there is something perceptible.” Just like Newton, he has washed away all of reality and had to sprinkle what we might call gold dust over his invisible spacetime so that places can be identified. He shows no awareness of Mach’s or Poincaré’s critiques of Newton’s concepts, both by then well known.

In his creation of general relativity, Einstein did, of course, retain Minkowski’s great innovation of light cones but his introduction of variable spacetime curvature only partially eliminated the need for Minkowski’s gold dust since in infinitesimal regions spacetime is Minkowskian. It is the universal glue that holds Einstein’s world together. However, since the glue is, apart from the light cones, featureless, one has to ask whether it can do the job. It may also be noted that many relativists are concerned that the field equations of general relativity allow an uncomfortably large number of solutions with many whose physicality seems questionable. The analysis of solutions that the _N_-body problem allows suggests that ‘purification’ of general relativity requires its ontology to be founded on recognisable things.

That could have far reaching consequences. Relative equilibria (see footnote 5) are determined holistically by the mass ratios of the particles and nothing else except for their being in Euclidean space. Until recently, only relatively simple few-particle examples like those in [11] or very uniform ones with many particles as found numerically in [15] were known. However, in 2021 Iizquierdo [16] found remarkable 1000-particle central configurations in two dimensions containing a profusion of filaments and voids. Louren C_(shape) co has recently found a very similar 5000-particle example [17] and numerous filaments for 1000 particles in three dimensions [18]. These results and also the fact that shapes as opposed to configurations have probabilities, which raises the question of the connection of those non-quantum probabilities with the quantum ones, suggest to me, as argued in the recent podcasts on my website, that the radical reductionism that Newton made the foundation of physics may have almost entirely hidden from physicists the true nature of reality and the universe.
